newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK govt backs CLP plan to decommission turbines.
newsitem.headline: HK govt backs CLP plan to decommission turbines.

text.p: China Light & Power Co Ltd's proposal to decommission gas turbines at its Castle Peak and Tsing Yi power stations has received government backing, Hong Kong's Secretary for Economic Services Stephen Ip said on Monday.

Ip told a Legislative Council panel meeting to discuss a reduction in excess power supply in Hong Kong, said the government did not agree with China Light's proposal to sell electricity to its competitor Hongkong Electric Holdings Ltd.
"We don't totally agree with CLP...I don't think that this is a solution for this imminent problem," he said.
The government asked China Light last November to submit a report on the cost of deferring the second phase of its Black Point power plant due to slowing growth in electricity demand in Hong Kong.

It its report, submitted in February, China Light said deferral of the construction of the Black Point power station could cost from HK$200 million to more than HK$1.5 billion in additional costs and proposed alternatives for reducing supply.
These alternatives were a transfer of power to Hongkong Electric Holdings and the decommissioning of some gas turbines at its Tsing Yi and Castle Peak power stations.
Ip said the government would decide within the next three weeks whether China Light needed to defer units five to eight of the Black Point project.
"I hope that in two to three weeks time we can form a view as what should be done whether to delay units five and six or seven and eight," he said.

Black Point consists of eight 312-megawatts units, two of which were commissioned in mid-1996 and two due to be switched on in mid-1997. The remaining four were due to be turned on at a rate of one a year until the year 2001.
Peter Littlewood, general manager strategic development at China Light, said the development of units five and six were far too advanced to defer.
"All we could do is delay commissioning," he said, adding that China Light did not believe it was in the interest of its customers.
"A deferral of units seven and eight is technically feasible but it would reduce the reserve margin in the long term," Littlewood added.
China Light said if it decommissioned the gas turbines, the reserve margin would decrease immediately by 10 percent.
The government said China Light would then not have enough electricity to sell to Hongkong Electric by the year 2003.
